0cf02ee21a6bca:
Two ancient traditions

While Europe was just beginning to document its medicine, India already had Ayurveda (c. 1500 BC) and China already had its own medical system based on bodily balance — both complete, with theories, diagnoses and treatments organized into extensive texts.

Ayurveda

Organized health around three "doshas" (bodily energies) that had to stay balanced, and already used surgery, specific diets and hundreds of medicinal plants with real effects documented through repeated observation.

Traditional Chinese medicine

Developed the idea of specific points on the body connected by "meridians" (acupuncture), and an approach that treated the whole person, not just the isolated symptom — an idea Western medicine took centuries to value again.

💡 What holds up and what doesn't: the holistic approach (looking at the whole person) of both systems is supported by modern medicine today. But many of their specific explanations (doshas, meridians as physical structures) haven't been confirmed by the scientific method — they're part of their history, not current medical evidence.
🌿 Some plants used in Ayurveda and Chinese medicine, like willow bark (a precursor to aspirin) or Artemisia annua (the basis of a modern malaria treatment), did turn out to have real active compounds — confirmed centuries later by modern chemistry.

0d0bf400f4bf4a:
The first heart transplant

On December 3, 1967, South African surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the first successful human heart transplant. The patient lived 18 days — short by today's standards, but an absolute milestone: it proved it was possible.

Seeing without cutting

The same era brought three technologies that radically changed medical diagnosis:

  • X-rays (refined and made widespread during this period): let you see bones and dense structures.
  • Ultrasound: uses sound waves to see soft tissue and organs in motion — key, for example, in monitoring pregnancy.
  • Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): uses magnetic fields to generate extremely detailed images of soft tissue, with no radiation.
📈 The combined result: better diagnoses, more precise surgeries, and less need to "open someone up to see what's going on" — something that, for almost all of medical history, was the only option.

The final result: decades of life gained

The combination of antibiotics, vaccines, safe surgery and imaging diagnosis raised global life expectancy from around 45 years to more than 70 years over the course of the 20th century — one of humanity's greatest collective achievements, almost invisible because it happened gradually.

From history to the practical

You've reached the most practical part of the course. The next modules are different from the previous ones: instead of history, you're going to learn what to do in real emergencies — information that, someday, could help you save a life.

A fact that changes your perspective

70% of cardiac arrests happen outside a hospital — at home, on the street, at work. In those moments, whoever is nearby (not a doctor, you) is the one who can make the difference between life and death, while professional help arrives.

⏱️ The key fact: the brain starts suffering irreversible damage from lack of oxygen between 4 and 6 minutes after cardiac arrest. The average ambulance takes longer than that to arrive. CPR applied by a bystander can triple the odds of survival while help is on the way.

You don't need to be a doctor

The following modules (CPR, bleeding and wounds, emergencies like heart attacks and strokes) are designed for anyone, with no prior medical knowledge. Read them calmly — it's not information you need to memorize perfectly, but you do need to have seen it once to recognize it if you ever really need it.

⚠️ This course teaches basic first aid for educational purposes. To get formally certified in CPR and first aid (recommended for everyone), look for a certified in-person course in your area — hands-on practice with a real instructor can't be replaced.

15cb0a8a0ed9c5: How to control bleeding, clean a wound properly and classify burns — and the common mistakes that make things worse.
1d34d74c4da08c:
Bleeding: direct pressure comes first

Facing a heavily bleeding wound, the most important and effective step is applying firm direct pressure on the wound with a clean cloth (or whatever you have available) for several minutes straight, without lifting it to "check" every so often.

❌ Common mistake: lifting the cloth every few seconds to see if it's stopped bleeding. That interrupts the clotting process and makes it bleed more, not less.

Wounds: clean before covering

A minor wound should be cleaned with clean (ideally running) water to remove dirt, and covered with a clean dressing. Avoid using alcohol or hydrogen peroxide directly on large open wounds — they can damage healthy tissue and irritate more than they disinfect.

Burns: the three degrees

  • First degree: just redness (like a mild sunburn). Treat with cool water (not ice) for several minutes.
  • Second degree: blisters and intense pain. Cool water, cover without popping the blisters, seek medical attention if it's extensive.
  • Third degree: whitish or charred skin, may hurt less due to nerve damage — it's a medical emergency, requiring immediate attention.
⚠️ Never apply direct ice, butter, toothpaste or home remedies to a burn — they're popular myths that make the skin damage worse.

00a6fb23f6369d: Recognizing the signs of a heart attack or stroke in time can save a life — and knowing what to do while the ambulance is on its way.
19de017f29a982:
Recognizing a heart attack

Classic heart attack signs include chest pain or tightness (which can radiate to the left arm, jaw or back), difficulty breathing, cold sweat and nausea. Important: in women, symptoms are sometimes more subtle — unusual fatigue, back or jaw pain without the classic chest pain.

Recognizing a stroke: the FAST method

A stroke is quickly recognized with the acronym FAST:

  • Face: ask them to smile — does one side of the face droop?
  • Arms: ask them to raise both arms — does one drift down on its own?
  • Speech: ask them to repeat a simple sentence — is their speech slurred?
  • Time: if there's ANY of these signs, it's time to call emergency services immediately.
⏰ In a stroke, "time is brain" — every minute without treatment means more neurons irreversibly damaged. Acting fast completely changes the outcome.

Seizures, fainting and severe allergies

During a seizure: don't hold the person down firmly, remove nearby dangerous objects, protect their head, and don't put anything in their mouth. For a simple faint: lay them down and raise their legs. For a severe allergic reaction (difficulty breathing, facial swelling): it's an emergency — call immediately.

💡 The ideal basic first-aid kit includes: sterile gauze and bandages, medical adhesive tape, disposable gloves, mild antiseptic, scissors, and your local emergency numbers saved somewhere visible.
